E7A01: Bistable = two stable states that it stays in: a flip-flop. It's the memory cell of digital logic.
E7A02: A decade counter outputs one pulse for every 10 input pulses: it divides by 10.
E7A03: Each flip-flop toggles once per two input pulses, so it divides by 2.
E7A04: Each flip-flop divides by 2. 2^4 = 16, so you need 4.
E7A05: Astable = no stable state, so it flips back and forth forever on its own (a free-running oscillator).
E7A06: Monostable = one stable state. Triggered, it flips for a set time, then returns (a one-shot).
E7A07: NAND = NOT-AND: the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.
E7A08: OR: the output is 1 if any input is 1.
E7A09: XNOR is the opposite of XOR: the output is 0 when exactly one input is 1 (inputs differ), and 1 when they match.
E7A10: A truth table lists every input combination and the matching output of a digital device.
E7A11: Positive logic: high voltage = 1, low voltage = 0.
E7B01: Classes by conduction angle: A = 360 deg, AB = more than 180 but less than 360 deg, B = 180 deg, C = less than 180 deg.
E7B02: Class D = switching amplifier, for high efficiency.
E7B03: A switching amplifier puts out square-ish waves full of harmonics, so it needs an output filter to remove them.
E7B04: Class A biases the transistor halfway between saturation and cutoff, so the signal can swing both ways.
E7B05: Stop parasitic oscillations with parasitic suppressors and/or by neutralizing the stage.
E7B06: Grounded-grid amplifiers have low input impedance (you drive the cathode), so they're easy to match to 50 ohms.
E7B07: SSB needs a linear amplifier. Class C distorts it and splatters (excessive bandwidth).
E7B08: A switch that's fully on (saturation) or fully off (cutoff) wastes almost no power, so switching amplifiers are efficient.
E7B09: An emitter follower has its output in phase with its input. Voltage gain is about 1, but it buffers impedance (high in, low out).
E7B10: R1 and R2 form a voltage divider from + to ground that sets the base bias.
E7B11: R3 in the emitter lead provides self bias (stabilizing negative feedback). C3 bypasses it for AC.
E7B12: Input to the base, output from the collector, emitter to ground through R3/C3: common emitter.
E7C01: Pi network (shaped like the letter pi): a capacitor to ground at the input, a capacitor to ground at the output, and an inductor in series between them. That's a low-pass.
E7C02: Series capacitors pass highs and a shunt inductor shorts lows to ground, so it's high-pass.
E7C03: Pi-L adds an inductor to the Pi, giving greater harmonic suppression.
E7C04: A matching network cancels the reactive part, then transforms the resistance to the value you want.
E7C05: Chebyshev: ripple in the passband, with a sharp cutoff. Butterworth is flat but rolls off more gently.
E7C06: Elliptical: extremely sharp cutoff, with notches in the stop band.
E7C07: Pi-L = a Pi network with an extra series inductor at the output.
E7C08: VHF/UHF radios often use helical filters as band-pass or notch filters.
E7C09: A crystal lattice filter is built from quartz crystals: high-Q, for low-level signals (IF filters).
E7C10: Repeater duplexers use cavity filters: very high Q, to handle closely spaced transmit and receive frequencies.
E7C11: Shape factor = how steep the skirts are (a ratio of bandwidths), so it measures adjacent-channel rejection.
E7D01: A linear regulator varies how much its control element conducts, to keep the output constant.
E7D02: A switchmode regulator varies the duty cycle of pulses fed into a filter.
E7D03: A Zener diode is a stable voltage reference.
E7D04: A three-terminal regulator (like the 7805) is a series regulator.
E7D05: A shunt regulator sits across (loads) the source and bleeds off the extra current to hold the voltage.
E7D06: Q1 is the series pass transistor: it controls the current to keep the output voltage constant.
E7D07: C2 sits across the Zener (D1) and bypasses ripple around it, keeping the reference clean.
E7D08: Pass transistor plus Zener reference, no switching: a linear voltage regulator.
E7D09: Battery run time = amp-hours / average current. For example, 100 Ah / 5 A = 20 hours.
E7D10: Switchers run at high frequency, so their transformers and filter parts are much smaller and lighter.
E7D11: An inverter converts DC (from the panel) to AC.
E7D12: Dropout voltage = the minimum input-to-output difference that still keeps regulation.
E7D13: Series regulator dissipation = (Vin - Vout) x output current. The voltage it drops, times the current through it.
E7D14: Equalizing resistors do all of these: balance the voltage across series caps, bleed them down safely, and give the supply a minimum load.
E7D15: A step-start circuit lets the filter capacitors charge gradually, avoiding a huge inrush current.
E7E01: FM phone: reactance modulation of an oscillator (not the final amp).
E7E02: A reactance modulator produces FM or PM by varying a capacitance.
E7E03: A frequency discriminator detects FM signals.
E7E04: SSB, filter method: a balanced modulator makes DSB with the carrier removed, then a filter removes one sideband.
E7E05: Pre-emphasis boosts the high audio frequencies at the transmitter.
E7E06: De-emphasis at the receiver undoes the transmitter's pre-emphasis, which makes FM receivers compatible with phase modulation (which boosts highs naturally).
E7E07: Baseband = the message signal's frequency range before modulation (for example, your voice audio).
E7E08: A mixer outputs both original frequencies plus their sum and difference.
E7E09: Overdriving a mixer creates spurious mixing products.
E7E10: An envelope detector is a diode that rectifies the RF, then a filter that smooths it. That's how AM is detected.
E7E11: SSB is demodulated by a product detector.
E7F01: Direct sampling: the ADC digitizes the RF directly, with no mixing to an IF.
E7F02: An adaptive DSP filter learns the noise and removes it.
E7F03: A Hilbert-transform filter makes the 90-degree phase shift used to generate SSB digitally.
E7F04: DSP SSB: combine signals in quadrature (90 deg apart, I and Q), so one sideband cancels.
E7F05: Nyquist: sample at least twice the highest frequency in the signal.
E7F06: 1 V / 1 mV = 1000 steps. 2^10 = 1024, so 10 bits is the minimum.
E7F07: An FFT converts the time domain to the frequency domain. That's how a waterfall display is made.
E7F08: Decimation lowers the sample rate by dropping samples.
E7F09: Before decimating, an anti-aliasing filter removes high frequencies that would otherwise alias down as false low frequencies.
E7F10: A direct-sampling SDR's maximum bandwidth is set by its sample rate (Nyquist).
E7F11: With no other noise, the smallest detectable signal is one ADC step: the reference voltage divided by 2^bits.
E7F12: FIR filters can delay all frequencies by the same amount (linear phase), so they don't distort the waveform.
E7F13: Taps are the incremental delays (stored samples) that the filter math combines.
E7F14: More taps make a sharper DSP filter.
E7G02: A cap across the feedback resistor shorts the feedback at high frequencies, so gain falls at highs: low-pass.
E7G04: Input offset voltage = the small differential input needed to bring the open-loop output to zero.
E7G05: To prevent ringing in an op-amp filter, keep both gain and Q modest.
E7G06: Gain-bandwidth = the frequency where the open-loop gain drops to 1.
E7G08: An ideal op-amp's gain doesn't vary with frequency (it's infinite everywhere).
E7G09: Gain = -RF / R1 = -10000 / 1000 = -10. Then -10 x 0.23 V = -2.3 V. Inverting, so it's negative.
E7G12: An op-amp is a high-gain, direct-coupled differential amplifier with very high input and very low output impedance.
E7H01: Common oscillators: Colpitts, Hartley, and Pierce. Taft, Fenner, and Beane are fake (Fenner and Beane come from Merrill Lynch, Pierce, Fenner and Smith).
E7H02: Microphonics = the oscillator's frequency shifting from mechanical vibration.
E7H03: A PLL: phase detector, low-pass (loop) filter, VCO, and a stable reference oscillator.
E7H04: Colpitts gets feedback through a capacitive divider. Memory hook: Colpitts = Capacitors, Hartley = tapped coil (Henries).
E7H05: Pierce gets feedback through a quartz crystal.
E7H06: A PLL can do frequency synthesis and FM demodulation.
E7H07: Reduce microphonics by mechanically isolating the oscillator from its enclosure.
E7H08: NP0 (C0G) capacitors have near-zero temperature coefficient, which reduces drift.
E7H09: Phase accumulator + lookup table + DAC + filter = a direct digital synthesizer (DDS).
E7H10: A DDS lookup table holds amplitude values that represent the waveform (a sine table).
E7H11: A DDS's main impurities are spurs at discrete frequencies, not broadband noise.
E7H12: A crystal hits its marked frequency only with the specified parallel load capacitance.
E7H13: All of these give microwave-grade accuracy and stability: a GPS reference, a rubidium standard, a temperature-controlled dielectric resonator.
